text: Middle East crisis ‘largest threat’ to energy security ever: International Energy Agency. # Middle East crisis ‘largest threat’ to energy security ever: International Energy Agency - The IEA said the Middle East crisis is the “largest threat” to energy security in history, after US and Israeli strikes on Iran and the Strait of Hormuz blockade disrupted oil exports. - Consumers are paying more as governments use extra supplies and alternative routes, but the IEA warned the crisis will leave “lasting marks” and cause higher prices and shortages. - In its World Energy Outlook, the IEA said oil demand may peak around 2030 in its middle case, while gas demand may rise until 2035; Birol said there is “no credible pathway” back to the old energy world. AI generated PARIS – The crisis in the Middle East sparked in February by the US and Israeli bombing of Iran has created the “largest threat” to energy security in history, the International Energy Agency (IEA) warned on Nov 19. The agency said in its flagship annual World Energy Outlook that consumers were increasingly footing the bill as the world runs out of ways to absorb the impact of the conflict on energy supplies. The crisis, just like previous energy shocks, would certainly leave “lasting marks”, the agency warned. Gulf countries have been struggling to export oil since Iran began blockading the Strait of Hormuz and targeting tankers in the area, following US and Israeli strikes that sparked the crisis in February. Despite attempts by the United States to escort vessels through the channel – which pre-crisis carried about one-fifth of global oil shipments, supply lines remain severely disrupted. “The Strait of Hormuz crisis has created the largest threat to energy security in history, one that dwarfs the scale of the oil shocks of the 1970s,” IEA executive director Fatih Birol wrote in his foreword to the report. He highlighted the efforts countries had taken to protect households, with producing nations bringing more supplies into the market and using alternative routes, and China buying less from international markets. “Governments have intervened to try and provide some shelter for consumers, but they have nonetheless faced higher prices and, in some cases, shortfalls of supply,” Birol wrote. The report said elsewhere that “increasingly it is falling to consumers – and high prices – to absorb the impact as other buffers are run down”. Birol had struck a more hopeful tone in July when he wrote that the oil market was still benefiting from “several cushioning factors”. ## ‘No pathway’ back The IEA’s report comes as nations meet for the COP31 climate talks in Turkey, with governments under pressure to tackle climate change after a year of searing heatwaves and wildfires in Europe, and deadly floods in Nepal. The agency uses three scenarios for its energy outlook: a cautious one takes into account policies that are currently in place, a middle scenario looks at “stated” government policies including measures that have yet to be adopted, and a third considers a world that reaches net zero emissions by 2050. In its middle scenario, the IEA forecasts that global oil demand will reach a peak around 2030 before a slow decline, while gas demand would increase until around 2035. For this report, it also adds two other scenarios based on what might happen if the Middle East crisis persists. “While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be,” Birol said in a press statement. “And I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before.” AFP
